parts.problem_md:
‘Throughout the play there is a battle between good and evil.’

Explore the theme of good versus evil in Macbeth.

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the play in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

In Macbeth, Shakespeare presents a conflict between good and evil, which drives the play from the very first scene to the final resolution. The theme is explored through the moral decline of Macbeth, the contrasting actions of noble characters like Banquo and Macduff and the larger impact of evil on the natural and social order of Scotland. The play shows that although evil can corrupt and destroy, it is ultimately defeated by the forces of good.

At the beginning of the play, Macbeth is introduced as a loyal and brave general. His heroic actions in the battle earn him high praise from the Captain, who calls him “brave Macbeth — well he deserves that name”. King Duncan also rewards him with the title of Thane of Cawdor. Macbeth’s alignment with good is clear at this stage, and Duncan’s praise, “I have begun to plant thee, and will labour / To make thee full of growing”, uses a metaphor to suggest that Macbeth will flourish under his rule. Structurally, this positive portrayal makes Macbeth’s later downfall more tragic and highlights the powerful influence of evil.

This influence of evil arrives with the Witches, whose prophecies ignite Macbeth’s ambition. Their greeting, “All hail, Macbeth! that shalt be king hereafter!” plants the idea of kingship in his mind and leads him to believe that he is destined to rule. However, Shakespeare presents the Witches as dangerous figures, aligned with the supernatural and the demonic. Banquo’s reaction to them is more cautious. He recognises that they may be trying to trap them: “The instruments of darkness tell us truths; / Win us with honest trifles, to betray’s / In deepest consequence”. This contrast between Macbeth and Banquo emphasises the moral choice available to them and shows Macbeth beginning to shift towards evil.

Despite his ambition, Macbeth initially struggles with the idea of murdering Duncan. In a soliloquy, he acknowledges the reasons not to go through with the act: Duncan is his guest, his kinsman and a virtuous king. Macbeth describes Duncan’s virtues as “plead[ing] like angels, trumpet-tongued”, suggesting that he is aware of the moral and spiritual consequences of the murder. However, Lady Macbeth’s manipulation proves decisive. She mocks his masculinity, “When you durst do it, then you were a man” and questions his courage, persuading him to commit the murder. Her influence shows how evil can be persuasive.

Once Macbeth kills Duncan, the balance changes in favour of evil. The natural world responds to this disruption: “By the clock ’tis day, / And yet dark night strangles the travelling lamp”. Shakespeare uses this image of darkness to show how Macbeth’s crime has upset the natural order. This would have resonated with a Jacobean audience, who believed in the Divine Right of Kings and the Great Chain of Being. A king was God’s chosen representative, so regicide was not only a political crime but a spiritual one as well.

As Macbeth becomes more tyrannical, Scotland suffers. He continues to commit atrocities, including the murder of Macduff’s family. In response, Macduff joins Malcolm, Duncan’s son, in raising an army to overthrow Macbeth. Macduff’s grief, “My wife and children’s ghosts will haunt me still”, is genuine, but he channels his sorrow into a desire for justice: “let grief / Convert to anger”. Macduff’s desire to “Bleed, bleed, poor country” shows that he is motivated not by personal gain but by the wish to restore peace and order.

The play ends with the defeat of Macbeth, marking the triumph of good. Macduff, representing justice and loyalty, kills Macbeth and declares that “the time is free”. This short statement signals the end of tyranny. Malcolm’s speech after Macbeth’s death mirrors Duncan’s earlier language, using the metaphor of planting again: “What’s more to do, / Which would be planted newly with the time”. This parallel in the language and structure shows that the natural order has been restored.

In conclusion, Macbeth presents the struggle between good and evil as a central theme. Shakespeare explores this conflict through characterisation, imagery and dramatic structure. While Macbeth succumbs to evil through ambition and persuasion, characters like Banquo, Macduff and Malcolm remain firm in their moral convictions. Ultimately, good triumphs, restoring order to Scotland and reaffirming the values of justice and rightful authority. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This is a confident and well-developed response that maintains a clear focus on the theme of good versus evil throughout. It presents a coherent and thoughtful argument, supported by relevant textual evidence and a secure understanding of character, narrative and structure. Analysis of language is insightful, particularly in relation to Macbeth’s soliloquies, the Witches’ influence and Shakespeare’s use of imagery and contrast. Structural features are explored effectively and contextual references, such as Jacobean beliefs in the Divine Right of Kings and the supernatural, are well integrated into the analysis. Overall, this response demonstrates strong conceptual understanding and meets the top-level criteria across all assessment objectives. > **[exam-tip]** > - Track how **Macbeth shifts** from a brave, honourable soldier to a ruthless, tyrannical murderer > - Explore how Shakespeare presents the **influence of evil** through the **Witches**, **Lady Macbeth**, and Macbeth’s **own ambition** > - Show how the theme of **good vs evil** is reflected in the fate of **Scotland **— chaos under Macbeth, order restored by Malcolm > - Contrast **Macbeth’s moral decline** with **Banquo’s integrity** and **Macduff’s loyalty** to highlight moral choices > - Reflect on how **soliloquies** reveal Macbeth’s inner conflict and growing obsession, exposing the **psychological effects of evil**

parts.problem_md:
How does Shakespeare present the character of Macbeth in the play?

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the play in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

Shakespeare presents Macbeth as a tragic figure who begins as a loyal and courageous soldier but descends into tyranny, driven by ambition, supernatural influence and manipulation. Macbeth’s journey is central to the play’s structure and themes and Shakespeare uses language, structure and form to reveal how ambition can corrupt even the most honourable.

At the beginning of the play, Macbeth is admired for his bravery. The Captain praises his role in battle: “brave Macbeth — well he deserves that name”. Duncan also rewards him with the title Thane of Cawdor, affirming Macbeth’s loyalty and worth. This honourable reputation is further emphasised when he is described through the metaphor as “Bellona’s bridegroom”, likening him to Mars, the Roman god of war. In Jacobean society, such loyalty to the king was sacred. Macbeth’s initial status as a brave, trustworthy noble makes his later downfall more tragic and shocking.

Macbeth’s transformation begins when he encounters the Witches. He is fascinated by their strange appearance, “What are these, / So wither’d, and so wild in their attire”, and immediately intrigued by their prophecies. Banquo observes that Macbeth “seems rapt withal”, showing how strongly he is affected. When the prophecy that he will be Thane of Cawdor proves true, Macbeth begins to believe he is destined to be king. However, Duncan names Malcolm as heir: “The Prince of Cumberland!”, which Macbeth sees as an obstacle. The idea of murder first takes hold, showing ambition beginning to override his loyalty.

Despite this, Macbeth initially struggles with the idea of killing Duncan. In a soliloquy, he reflects on Duncan’s goodness and his own responsibilities as “kinsman”, “subject” and “host”. He notes Duncan’s virtues “Will plead like angels, trumpet-tongued”, using religious imagery to show the moral weight of the crime. At first, Macbeth concludes: “We will proceed no further in this business”, showing that his conscience still has power. However, Lady Macbeth mocks his hesitation, questioning his courage: “When you durst do it, then you were a man”. Her manipulation proves successful and Macbeth’s resolve collapses. A Jacobean audience might have been surprised to see a woman exerting such power over her husband, defying expectations of female submissiveness.

Once Duncan is murdered, Macbeth is overwhelmed by fear and guilt. He thinks he hears a voice cry, “Sleep no more! / Macbeth does murder sleep”, symbolising a loss of peace and innocence. Fear begins to dominate him, and he starts to kill to protect himself. He arranges the murder of Banquo not out of necessity but because of jealousy: “For Banquo’s issue have I filed my mind”. Macbeth has no heir and resents that Banquo’s children will inherit the throne.

Banquo’s ghost haunts Macbeth at a banquet, exposing the psychological effects of his crimes. He shouts, “Thou canst not say I did it. Never shake / Thy gory locks at me!”, showing his guilt and loss of control. This is a striking contrast to the fearless warrior portrayed at the start of the play. Shakespeare structures the play so that Macbeth’s psychological unravelling mirrors his moral decline.

When he hears of Lady Macbeth’s death, Macbeth expresses a bleak outlook on life: “Life’s but a walking shadow… a poor player / That struts and frets his hour upon the stage / And then is heard no more”. He views life as meaningless, shaped by ambition and futility. He also begins to doubt the Witches’ promises: “I pull in resolution and begin / To doubt th’ equivocation of the fiend / That lies like truth”, showing his realisation that he has been deceived.

Despite everything, Macbeth regains some bravery in the final act. He declares, “I’ll fight till from my bones my flesh be hack’d”, and asks for his armour, echoing the fearless soldier we saw at the start. He also says, “I had almost forgot the taste of fear”, suggesting he has become numb to emotion. Though he remains defiant, his downfall is inevitable. Indeed, Macbeth’s tragic fall results from his attempt to alter the natural and divine order. According to the Great Chain of Being and Divine Right of Kings, it was sinful to challenge the monarchy. Macbeth’s regicide brings chaos and leads to his destruction. His death allows order to be restored.

In conclusion, Shakespeare presents Macbeth as a tragic figure destroyed by ambition, manipulation and supernatural temptation. From noble beginnings to tragic end, Macbeth’s story serves as a warning of how quickly power can corrupt and how defying the natural order brings only ruin. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This is a focused and well-structured response that explores the character of Macbeth with clarity and precision. The essay traces Macbeth’s development from loyal soldier to tyrant effectively, using a clear line of argument supported by well-chosen textual references. Analysis of language is perceptive, particularly in the discussion of Macbeth’s soliloquies, the impact of the Witches and Lady Macbeth’s persuasive rhetoric. The response also comments thoughtfully on dramatic structure and form, showing understanding of how Macbeth’s mental and moral deterioration unfolds. > > Contextual references, such as Jacobean views on kingship, gender roles and the supernatural are integrated naturally into the analysis and used to deepen the interpretation. Overall, this essay demonstrates a strong conceptual grasp of the play and meets the criteria for the highest level across all assessment objectives. > **[exam-tip]** > - Track how **Macbeth shifts** from a **brave, noble soldier** to a **paranoid **and **violent tyrant** > - Explore how Shakespeare presents **ambition** as Macbeth’s fatal flaw, influenced by **supernatural forces** and **Lady Macbeth’s manipulation** > - Show how **Macbeth’s inner conflict** is revealed through his **soliloquies**, especially when he hesitates over killing Duncan > - Contrast Macbeth’s **early loyalty** with his later **betrayals and murders** to highlight his **moral collapse** > - Reflect on how **guilt and fear** affect Macbeth’s mental state, particularly in scenes like the **banquet with Banquo’s ghost** > - Link Macbeth’s downfall to **Jacobean beliefs** about **the Divine Right of Kings** and the **Great Chain of Being** to show how his actions bring about **chaos **and **retribution**

parts.problem_md:
In what ways does Macduff contribute to Macbeth’s downfall in the play?

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the play in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

In Macbeth, Shakespeare presents Macduff as a critical element in Macbeth’s downfall. A noble and loyal character, Macduff’s commitment to justice, his suspicion of Macbeth and his eventual decision to avenge the murder of his family all contribute to the tyrant’s defeat. Through Macduff, Shakespeare explores themes of loyalty, justice and the restoration of order, using language, structure and form to contrast Macduff with Macbeth and highlight the moral consequences of ambition and betrayal.

Macduff first emerges as a loyal soldier and committed servant of King Duncan. When he discovers Duncan’s murdered body, he reacts with horror and sorrow: “O horror, horror, horror”, calling it a “Most sacrilegious murder”. The adjective “sacrilegious” reflects the Jacobean belief in the Divine Right of Kings, where killing a monarch was not only treason but a crime against God. Macduff recognises this immediately, unlike others who appear more focused on practical matters. His strong moral compass is one of the qualities that sets him apart and foreshadows his future role in exposing and defeating Macbeth.

From early on, Macduff is suspicious of Macbeth. After Macbeth kills Duncan’s guards, allegedly out of anger, Macduff questions his motives: “Wherefore did you so?” His scepticism is further emphasised when he chooses not to attend Macbeth’s coronation, showing his unwillingness to support someone he distrusts. This resistance to blindly following the new king marks him as a character guided by conscience rather than ambition, forming a structural contrast with Macbeth’s rapid descent into tyranny.

Shakespeare presents Macduff as a foil to Macbeth. While Macbeth is consumed by self-interest and willing to kill to secure power, Macduff acts selflessly to protect Scotland. He travels to England to seek help from Malcolm and the English king, leaving his family behind. This action, while noble, leads to devastating consequences as Macbeth orders the murder of Macduff’s wife and children. Lady Macduff condemns his absence, saying, “His flight was madness” and that “He wants the natural touch” suggesting he lacks human feeling. However, Shakespeare later reveals Macduff’s profound grief, reinforcing his humanity and honour.

Macduff’s reaction to the news of his family’s death is deeply emotional. He says, “My wife and children’s ghosts will haunt me still” and vows to turn his grief into revenge. This personal loss fuels his determination to bring Macbeth down, yet his actions are not purely vengeful as they are also about restoring rightful order to Scotland. When Malcolm tests Macduff’s loyalty, Macduff is distraught at the thought of further corruption: “Bleed, bleed, poor country!” This line uses personification to show his deep concern for Scotland.

Macduff’s role becomes even more significant as the play reaches its climax. One of the Witches’ prophecies states that “none of woman born / Shall harm Macbeth” which gives Macbeth a false sense of invincibility. However, during their final confrontation, Macduff reveals that Macduff was “from his mother’s womb / Untimely ripped”. The revelation that Macduff was born by Caesarean section turns the prophecy against Macbeth and leads to his downfall.

In their final battle, Macduff declares, “My voice is in my sword” indicating that he lets action speak for justice. His resolve and righteousness contrast with Macbeth’s desperation and fading courage. Macduff ultimately kills Macbeth, fulfilling the prophecy and ending the tyrant’s rule. In doing so, he restores order to Scotland. He supports Malcolm’s claim to the throne, saying, “I see thee compassed with thy kingdom’s pearl”, which symbolises Malcolm’s noble supporters and the return of rightful leadership.

Shakespeare’s use of structure and form frames Macduff as the moral centre of the play. From the moment he suspects Macbeth to the final battle, Macduff’s journey is one of justice and loyalty. His role mirrors the structure of the tragic hero’s fall for while Macbeth falls from greatness through ambition, Macduff rises through honour and sacrifice. His presence in the final scenes of the play restores the natural order, fulfilling the expectations of a tragic resolution. For a Jacobean audience, Macduff represents the ideal nobleman: loyal to king and country, respectful of divine authority and unafraid to challenge evil.

In conclusion, Macduff contributes to Macbeth’s downfall through his loyalty, suspicion, personal loss and pursuit of justice. Shakespeare uses him as a foil to Macbeth and as a symbol of the righteous force that restores moral and political order. Through powerful language, structure and contextual relevance, Macduff’s role is essential in bringing the tragedy to its necessary end. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This is a focused and well-structured response that clearly addresses the ways in which Macduff contributes to Macbeth’s downfall. The essay presents a coherent and thoughtful argument, demonstrating a secure understanding of character, theme and plot. There is a strong focus on Macduff’s moral integrity, his contrast with Macbeth and his role in restoring order. Analysis of language is perceptive, particularly in relation to Macduff’s emotional responses and his use of powerful imagery. The response also comments effectively on structure and form, especially the use of Macduff as a foil. > > Contextual understanding is integrated well, with relevant references to the Divine Right of Kings, Jacobean beliefs and expectations of loyalty. Overall, this is a confident and well-developed essay that meets the criteria for the top mark range across all assessment objectives. > **[exam-tip]** > - Track how **Macduff’s loyalty** to Duncan and Scotland contrasts with **Macbeth’s betrayal and ambition** > - Explore how Shakespeare presents Macduff as a **moral force** through his emotional reactions, powerful language and sense of **justice** > - Show how **Macduff’s suspicion** of Macbeth builds early tension and positions him as a threat to Macbeth’s power > - Reflect on how Macduff’s **grief and loss** fuel his determination to seek **revenge**, leading to Macbeth’s ultimate defeat > - Contrast **Macduff’s honesty and courage** with Macbeth’s paranoia and tyranny to highlight Shakespeare’s use of character as **foils**

parts.problem_md:
‘Shakespeare makes great use of symbols, such as weather and blood.’

Explore the significance of symbols in Macbeth.

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the play in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

In Macbeth, Shakespeare makes powerful use of symbolism to explore major themes such as guilt, evil, disruption to the natural order and the struggle between good and evil. Symbols such as blood, weather, animals, light and darkness, sleep, and water help to deepen the audience’s understanding of character motivations and reinforce the play’s tragic and moral aspects. These recurring images are woven through the language, structure and form of the play and would have held particular resonance for a Jacobean audience.

One of the most prominent symbols in the play is blood, which represents guilt and the psychological consequences of murder. After Macbeth kills Duncan, he looks at his hands in horror: “What hands are here?” and later declares, “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?” The hyperbolic image of the sea turning red emphasises how deeply stained with guilt Macbeth feels. In contrast, Lady Macbeth initially believes that “A little water clears us of this deed”, but her confidence unravels later when she is seen obsessively rubbing her hands in her sleep, crying, “Out, damned spot!” This repeated symbolism of blood and water shows how guilt cannot be easily washed away and reflects the psychological torment that follows immoral actions. While water is used throughout the play to attempt to cleanse guilt, it has contextual links with witch trials, as floating on water was believed to be a sign of witchcraft. This connection adds another layer of irony to Lady Macbeth’s final attempts to wash her guilt away.

Weather is also symbolic throughout the play, particularly in connection with the Witches and unnatural events. The play begins with thunder and lightning, establishing a mood of foreboding. Each time the Witches appear, stormy weather follows, “When shall we three meet again / In thunder, lightning, or in rain?”, linking them to chaos and evil. In contrast, when King Duncan arrives at Macbeth’s castle, the weather is described as “Nimbly and sweetly” symbolising his goodness and the natural order he represents. The disruption of this order is mirrored by unnatural weather later in the play, such as when “dark night strangles the travelling lamp”, showing that the world itself reacts to Duncan’s murder.

Similarly, animal imagery is used to convey the breakdown of the natural order and to mirror characters’ states of mind. After Duncan’s murder, Ross notes that an owl has killed a falcon, “A falcon… / Was by a mousing owl hawked at and killed”. This unnatural reversal symbolises Macbeth, a lower-ranking nobleman, killing the king. The disturbance also spreads to Duncan’s horses, who break out of their stalls and eat each other, which is another clear sign of chaos. Later, Lady Macduff uses a bird metaphor to condemn Macduff’s abandonment: “the poor wren… will fight / Her young ones in her nest, against the owl”, casting Macbeth as the predatory owl and herself as the small, helpless bird. Animal imagery thus links to broader themes of disorder and destruction.

Light and darkness also serve as opposing forces throughout the play. Light is associated with goodness and virtue, as seen when Duncan says “Signs of nobleness, like stars, shall shine / On all deservers”. In contrast, Macbeth seeks darkness to conceal his ambitions: “Stars, hide your fires; / Let not light see my black and deep desires”. Lady Macbeth, too, calls upon the night: “Come, thick night”, hoping that darkness will mask her evil intentions. Later, in her sleepwalking scene, she carries a candle suggesting that in her madness, she now fears the darkness she once embraced. Shakespeare uses light and dark not just as imagery, but to symbolise internal moral conflict.

Sleep functions as another important symbol, representing innocence and peace. After murdering Duncan, Macbeth claims to hear a voice cry: “Sleep no more! Macbeth does murder sleep”. This reflects his sense of having destroyed not only Duncan’s rest but also his own. As the play progresses, both Macbeth and Lady Macbeth are increasingly disturbed by sleeplessness and nightmares. Shakespeare connects sleep to conscience as those with guilt cannot rest, while the innocent, like Duncan or Banquo’s son Fleance, are associated with peaceful sleep.

In conclusion, Shakespeare’s use of symbolism in Macbeth is central to its meaning. Symbols such as blood, weather, darkness and sleep are not only repeated throughout the play but serve to reveal character, reinforce themes and reflect the disruption of the natural and moral order. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This is a well-developed and thoughtful response that effectively explores the significance of symbolism in Macbeth. The essay maintains a clear focus on the question throughout, offering a coherent argument supported by a wide range of relevant examples. Analysis of language is detailed, especially in relation to blood, weather, light and darkness and there is confident discussion of how these symbols reflect character development and moral decline. Structural points are well made, showing how key symbolic moments mark turning points in the play. > > Contextual references, such as Jacobean beliefs about kingship, witchcraft and the natural order, are integrated well to enhance the analysis. Overall, this response demonstrates a strong conceptual understanding and meets the criteria for the top band across all assessment objectives. > **[exam-tip]** > - Track how symbols like **blood**, **weather**, **light/darkness** and **sleep** reflect characters’ **guilt**, **ambition** and **moral collapse** > - Explore how Shakespeare uses **symbolism to signal key turning points**, such as Duncan’s murder or Lady Macbeth’s breakdown > - Show how **blood** and **water** are linked to the theme of **guilt and cleansing**, particularly in Macbeth and Lady Macbeth’s language > - Reflect on how **light and darkness** symbolise **good and evil** and how characters use them to **hide or expose their intentions** > - Analyse how **unnatural animal behaviour **and **weather** symbolise the **disruption of the natural order** caused by Macbeth’s actions

parts.problem_md:
Captain: ‘The merciless Macdonald — / Worthy to be a rebel…’

Discuss the theme of betrayal in Macbeth.

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the play in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

In Macbeth, Shakespeare explores betrayal as a devastating force, affecting not only political power but also personal relationships and moral integrity. Through acts of treachery against individuals and against Scotland itself, the play highlights how betrayal leads to guilt, grief and tragedy. Many characters suffer as a result of betrayal and Shakespeare encourages sympathy for them through their language, actions and the consequences they face.

One of the first acts of betrayal in the play is committed by the Thane of Cawdor, who supports the Norwegian army against his own king. King Duncan, unaware of his disloyalty until it is too late, expresses sorrow that trust can be so easily broken: “He was a gentleman on whom I built / An absolute trust”. This line foreshadows Duncan’s misplaced trust in Macbeth, who is rewarded with the traitor’s title. Duncan’s generosity and honesty make him a deeply sympathetic figure. When Macbeth murders him, the act is not only a betrayal of loyalty but of hospitality and kinship. Macbeth himself reflects that Duncan’s “virtues / Will plead like angels”, a simile that heightens the audience’s sense of Duncan’s goodness and the horror of the crime. In Jacobean England, betrayal, especially of a monarch, was seen as a deadly sin, disrupting the Divine Right of Kings and the Great Chain of Being.

Banquo also becomes a victim of betrayal. Though he receives prophecies similar to Macbeth’s, he chooses not to act dishonourably, declaring he must keep his “allegiance clear”. His integrity contrasts sharply with Macbeth’s ambition. Despite this, Macbeth views Banquo as a threat and arranges for his murder. When the murderers attack, Banquo exclaims, “O, treachery!”, a powerful reminder of how he has been betrayed. Furthermore, given that Banquo was believed by King James I to be his ancestor, Shakespeare’s sympathetic portrayal may have been a political compliment to the king.

Macduff is another character who evokes sympathy through betrayal. Although his decision to leave Scotland and support Malcolm is patriotic, it leads to the murder of his innocent family. Lady Macduff calls his departure “madness” and says, “Our fears do make us traitors”, suggesting that even good intentions can appear as betrayal. Her bitter complaint, “Wisdom! — to leave his wife, to leave his babes”, emphasises her sense of abandonment. When Macduff learns of their deaths, he is devastated. His reaction, “all my pretty chickens and their dam / At one fell swoop?”, uses a metaphor to express his loss. His grief is raw and sincere and he blames himself: “Sinful Macduff, / They were all struck for thee!” This moment of guilt deepens audience sympathy and underscores the personal cost of betrayal.

While Macbeth is the play’s main betrayer, Shakespeare also invites a degree of sympathy for him. Early in the play, Macbeth is torn between ambition and loyalty. In a soliloquy, he considers Duncan’s virtues and his own roles as “kinsman” and “host”, clearly recognising the moral weight of murder. Yet under the influence of the Witches and Lady Macbeth, he proceeds. As the play progresses, Macbeth becomes increasingly isolated and haunted. After Lady Macbeth’s death, he responds not with grief but weary resignation: “She should have died hereafter”. This line shows how emotionally numb he has become, consumed by guilt and despair.

Lady Macbeth herself also elicits sympathy. Initially strong and persuasive, she unravels under the weight of guilt. In her sleepwalking scene, she imagines blood on her hands, “What, will these hands ne’er be clean?” and obsessively replays the events of Duncan’s murder. Her death is widely believed to be a suicide and her mental decline reflects the consequences of betrayal not just of others, but of conscience and morality. The audience may feel pity for her as someone who encouraged betrayal, but ultimately could not live with its cost.

In conclusion, Shakespeare presents betrayal in Macbeth as a destructive force that corrupts individuals and tears apart families, friendships and the natural order itself. While Macbeth is the central figure who betrays king, country and conscience, it is the impact of his betrayal on others, Duncan, Banquo, Macduff and Lady Macduff, that evokes the greatest sympathy. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This is a perceptive and well-developed response that maintains a consistent focus on the theme of betrayal and its emotional and moral consequences. The essay presents a thoughtful and coherent argument, supported by a wide range of relevant examples and close textual analysis. There is insightful discussion of character and motivation, particularly in relation to Duncan, Banquo, Macduff and Lady Macduff and a nuanced exploration of how sympathy is generated through Shakespeare’s language and structure. > > Contextual understanding is effective, with well-integrated references to Jacobean beliefs, such as the Divine Right of Kings and the Great Chain of Being. Overall, this is a confident response that fulfils the top-level criteria across all assessment objectives. > **[exam-tip]** > - Track how **betrayal drives the plot**, beginning with the Thane of Cawdor and ending with **Macbeth’s downfall** > - Explore how Shakespeare uses **dramatic irony** and **language of trust** to heighten the impact of betrayal, especially in Duncan’s interactions with Macbeth > - Show how betrayal leads to **emotional consequences**, particularly for **Banquo**, **Macduff** and **Lady Macduff**, and how this evokes **sympathy** > - Analyse how betrayal is not only political but also **deeply personal**, damaging relationships > - Contrast characters like **Macduff and Banquo**, who remain loyal, with Macbeth and Lady Macbeth, who **abandon their morals for power**

parts.problem_md:
Discuss the presentation of one character you sympathise with in the play.

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the play in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

In Macbeth, Shakespeare presents Banquo as a noble and loyal figure whose resistance to temptation and unjust death make him one of the most sympathetic characters in the play. While others around him give in to ambition and deceit, Banquo remains honourable, cautious and morally grounded. Through his language, behaviour and the way other characters treat him, Shakespeare encourages the audience to admire and pity him, especially as his murder reflects the growing corruption in Scotland under Macbeth’s rule.

Banquo is introduced early in the play as Macbeth’s fellow soldier and equal in battle. Like Macbeth, he receives a prophecy from the Witches, but unlike Macbeth, he remains suspicious of them. While Macbeth is “rapt” with attention, Banquo warns, “The instruments of darkness tell us truths... to betray’s / In deepest consequence”. This warning shows Banquo’s wisdom and moral awareness. He immediately senses danger, even when promised greatness. His scepticism stands in contrast to Macbeth’s eagerness, marking him as a character guided by caution and principle rather than ambition. This reluctance to trust the supernatural adds to his noble image.

Banquo’s refusal to betray King Duncan also contributes to the sympathy he inspires. When Macbeth tries to involve him in a private conversation about the Witches, Banquo responds, “So I lose none / In seeking to augment it”, meaning he will not gain power if it costs him his honour. Shakespeare presents Banquo as someone who could choose to chase power but consciously decides not to. This choice seals his fate, however, as Macbeth sees him as a threat, not only because of the prophecy that Banquo’s descendants will be kings, but because Banquo’s honour contrasts so sharply with Macbeth’s guilt.

The decision to murder Banquo is one of Macbeth’s most chilling acts. It marks a turning point in his moral descent, as he plans it without consulting Lady Macbeth and does so purely to secure his power. Macbeth describes Banquo as “royalty of nature” and notes his “dauntless temper” revealing that he envies Banquo’s natural leadership. The audience sees that Macbeth recognises Banquo’s goodness, yet chooses to destroy him. When Banquo realises what is happening, he cries, “O, treachery!”, a powerful single line that encapsulates his shock and betrayal. This moment evokes strong sympathy, as Banquo dies because he remains loyal and refuses to act unjustly.

Banquo’s murder is made even more tragic because of its impact on his son, Fleance. Although Fleance escapes, he is forced to flee alone into the night. Shakespeare’s decision to have Fleance survive suggests that Banquo’s line may still continue, but the emotional toll of Banquo’s death on his family is clear. Banquo’s murder symbolises the complete breakdown of morality in Macbeth’s Scotland. King James I believed he was descended from Banquo, and Shakespeare’s sympathetic portrayal of him as honourable and betrayed would have pleased the monarch. Banquo’s association with future kings, as the Witches predict, reinforces his lasting importance and justifies the audience’s admiration and pity.

Even in death, Banquo continues to influence the play’s events. His ghost appears at Macbeth’s banquet, shaking its “gory locks” at him. This haunting image is a manifestation of Macbeth’s guilt and mental instability. It also reminds the audience of Banquo’s unjust death and strengthens the sense of injustice. Macbeth’s terrified reaction, “quit my sight!”, reveals his inner torment and through this, Shakespeare highlights Banquo’s enduring moral power. For a Jacobean audience, the ghost may also represent a soul denied rest, further deepening the pathos around Banquo’s fate.

Structurally, Banquo’s role highlights the contrast between ambition and restraint. Both he and Macbeth begin the play as loyal warriors and receive prophecies, but only Macbeth acts on them violently. Banquo’s quiet dignity and inner strength are a foil to Macbeth’s moral collapse. Shakespeare uses this contrast to heighten the audience’s sympathy for Banquo, who dies precisely because he resists temptation. His story serves as a tragic example of how goodness is punished in a corrupt world.

In conclusion, Banquo is presented as a principled and courageous character whose moral strength contrasts sharply with Macbeth’s corruption. Shakespeare encourages the audience to sympathise with Banquo through his loyalty, his unjust death and the lasting legacy he leaves behind. parts.problem_md:
Explore the theme of ambition in Macbeth.

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the play in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Shakespeare presents ambition as a dangerous, corrupting force that drives Macbeth from loyal hero to murderous tyrant, and which ultimately destroys him.

Shakespeare shows that ambition is Macbeth’s only real motive for murder. In soliloquy he admits he has nothing spurring him on but “Vaulting ambition which o’erleaps itself”. The metaphor of a rider vaulting so hard that he falls off the other side warns that excessive ambition destroys itself. The soliloquy form lets the audience hear Macbeth’s private conscience, so we see that he knows the murder is wrong even as ambition pushes him on. For a Jacobean audience, who believed kings were chosen by God, this ambition to seize the throne was not only a crime but a sin against the natural order.

Shakespeare places the witches at the very start to show how this ambition is awakened. Their prophecy that Macbeth “shalt be king hereafter” plants the idea, yet Shakespeare leaves it unclear whether they create his ambition or simply reveal what is already there. By having Banquo react with caution while Macbeth is immediately gripped, Shakespeare uses contrast to suggest the ambition is Macbeth’s own. King James I’s belief in the genuine danger of witchcraft would have made this supernatural temptation truly frightening for the original audience.

Shakespeare also shows that ambition makes Macbeth deceitful, forcing him to hide his true self. When his path to the throne is blocked by Malcolm being named heir, Macbeth asks the “Stars, hide your fires” so that light will not “see my black and deep desires”. The metaphor of light and darkness shows that Macbeth already knows his ambition is shameful and must be concealed, even from himself. This aside, spoken while Duncan stands nearby, lets the audience share a guilty secret the King cannot see, building dramatic irony. To a Jacobean audience, plotting against an anointed king — only a year or so after the Gunpowder Plot to murder their own king — would have made these “black” desires feel like a real and present treason.

Ambition is not Macbeth’s alone. Lady Macbeth is at first the more ruthless, fearing that he is “too full o’th’ milk of human kindness” to seize the crown. The image of milk presents kindness as something soft she wants to drain out of him. She urges him to “be the serpent under’t”, hiding cruelty beneath a fair face, and calls on dark spirits to strip away any womanly pity that might stop her. Shakespeare uses her to show ambition overriding nature itself, and in a patriarchal society a woman so driven by ambition would have seemed deeply unnatural and disturbing.

Shakespeare also shows that ambition, once acted on, can never be satisfied. After killing Duncan, Macbeth murders again and again — Banquo, then Macduff’s family — to protect his crown, and his ambition curdles into paranoia and tyranny. Shakespeare uses the disordered natural world, where “darkness does the face of earth entomb”, to mirror the moral chaos that ambition has unleashed on Scotland. The murder of a divinely appointed king was believed to upset the whole universe, which is why nature itself seems to rebel.

By the end, ambition has brought Macbeth nothing. His wife is dead and his enemies are closing in, and he reflects bitterly that life is no more than a “brief candle”, soon snuffed out. The metaphor shows how ambition has hollowed out his existence until it feels empty and meaningless. Shakespeare’s tragic structure ensures that ambition leads only to isolation and despair, and Macbeth dies cursing the prophecies that first stirred him. The restoration of the rightful king, Malcolm, reaffirms the natural order that ambition tried to overturn, sending the Jacobean audience a clear warning.

Through soliloquy, the supernatural and the collapse of natural order, Shakespeare presents ambition as a force that promises greatness but delivers ruin. Macbeth’s fall warns that ambition, when it ignores conscience and the proper order of things, destroys not only the ambitious person but everything around them.
